items.item: A pointer to a trait object is two parts: a pointer to the concrete data, and a pointer to a vtable

at.step: Two words, not one

items.item: The vtable holds one function pointer per method of the trait (and its supertraits) that the concrete type implements

at.step: What's actually inside the second word?

items.item: Calling a method on a trait object loads a function pointer from the vtable at run time and invokes it indirectly (late binding)

at.step: Calling through it is late binding

items.item: A dyn-compatible trait's associated functions must each be either dispatchable from a trait object or explicitly marked non-dispatchable

at.step: A method that takes Self by value can't go in the vtable

items.item: A dispatchable method must take no type parameters and must not use Self except as its own receiver's type

at.step: A method that takes Self by value can't go in the vtable

items.item: A method is made explicitly non-dispatchable (excluded from the vtable) by adding a where Self: Sized bound to it

at.step: One bound excludes just that method

items.item: Dyn compatibility is the Reference's current name for what was formerly called object safety

at.deep: Internals: the vtable, dyn compatibility, and what optimization can't fix

items.item: Upcasting trait objects to supertraits was stabilized in Rust 1.86.0, released 2025-04-03

at.step: Widening to the parent trait, directly

items.item: The fat pointer itself is the fixed, one-time cost of using dyn Trait at all (one extra word per reference or Box); it is paid once per pointer, not once per call, and is not where most of the running-cost difference against monomorphization actually comes from

at.step: Two words, not one

items.item: The vtable is built once per concrete type at compile time (not once per value at run time); every value of that concrete type behind a dyn Trait pointer shares the same vtable, only the data pointer differs between them

at.step: What's actually inside the second word?

items.item: Late binding means the optimizer genuinely cannot know, at compile time, which concrete implementation a given dyn Trait call will reach, because that is decided by whichever data pointer happens to be paired with the vtable pointer at run time

at.step: Calling through it is late binding

items.item: Raising optimization level cannot remove a vtable call the way it removes a monomorphized call's overhead; the lost inlining is structural, not a missed optimization, because inlining requires knowing the callee at compile time and a vtable call by definition does not

at.step: The cost isn't the indirect call

items.item: The reputation that dyn Trait is slow because of "the indirect call" undersells the real cost and oversells a fix: removing the indirection (e.g. with enum dispatch) helps, but the inlining lost at every dyn Trait call site is usually the larger effect on real workloads with small, frequently-called methods

at.deep: Internals: the vtable, dyn compatibility, and what optimization can't fix

items.item: A by-value Self method is excluded not because Self is somehow forbidden, but because the callee's own code would need to know Self's concrete size to receive it by value, and a fat pointer deliberately erases exactly that information

at.step: A method that takes Self by value can't go in the vtable

items.item: A generic method is dyn-incompatible for a related but separate reason: a vtable has one fixed function-pointer slot per method, and a generic method would need a different slot per instantiation, which the vtable's fixed shape cannot express

at.deep: Internals: the vtable, dyn compatibility, and what optimization can't fix

items.item: Adding where Self: Sized to one method doesn't make the trait object able to call that method; it makes the compiler build the vtable without a slot for it at all, so the trait object simply never offers it, while every other dyn-compatible method still does

at.step: One bound excludes just that method

items.item: Upcasting is a coercion at the type-checking level, not a run-time conversion; a SubTrait's vtable is laid out so a SuperTrait's slots can be read directly out of it, with no new vtable built and no detour through the concrete type

at.step: Widening to the parent trait, directly

items.item: Enum dispatch's real trade is closedness for structure: a match on a known, fixed set of variants gives the compiler everything it needs to inline each arm, at the literal cost that adding a new implementor means editing the enum, which dyn Trait never requires

at.step: A closed list, matched by hand
